AW : don't forget to open the tidyverse dataset
1. Open the starwars dataset (located in tidyverse)
```{r}
data(starwars)
```

2. Create a scatter plot of character's height and mass. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass)) + geom_point()
```

2a. Change the color and shape of the points in your scatter plot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass)) + geom_point(shape = 4, color = "royalblue")
```

3. Add Homeworld as a third variable to your scatterplot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, fill = homeworld)) + geom_point(shape = 4)
```

3a. What do you notice about the graph? (e.g. describe what you see)

This graph is pretty ugly! Adding homeworld as a third variable by color is not the best decision, because there's so many homeworlds that the graph just kind of is a small blob featuring a gigantic legend of homeworlds.

4. Make a boxplot of height. 
```{r}

ggplot(starwars, aes(height))+ geom_boxplot()
```

5. Make a boxplot of height for each species present in the data. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, species))+ geom_boxplot()
```

5a. change the appearance of your graph in at least 3 ways. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, species))+ geom_boxplot(fill = "firebrick4", color = "honeydew4") + labs(x= "Height in cm", y = "Species") + ggtitle("Species and Height in Star Wars Characters")
```

6. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from viridis.
```{r}
library(viridisLite)
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, fill = homeworld)) + geom_histogram() + scale_fill_viridis_b(option = "plasma", discrete = TRUE)
```

7.Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from RColorBrewer.
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(mass, height, color = hair_color)) + geom_point() + scale_color_brewer(palette = "Purples")
```

8. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph using facet_wrap
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color = gender)) + geom_boxplot()+ facet_wrap(~gender)
```
